about: The refusal table of the UML-view editing spec (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-12-c4-uml-view-editing.md §5.1), copied verbatim, plus the proposed row link-self (plan Task 33), as the alignment review (CP-4) of Task 33 Step 6 left it: interfaces/add-element and interfaces/neighbour name "a context, container, or component view" instead of "a C4 view", and same-element-instances speaks of instances, not copies. The sentence of interfaces/declared-elsewhere for an addition on a neighbour, which names no interface yet, is Task 42b's (Ruling U12), marked for the CP-4 wording review. ‹…› are placeholders. uml-refusals.test.js fills every row with `fill` and compares it with parts.umlRefusals.verdict; a row whose words depend on the model (`cases`) is compared case by case with the texts written out below from the spec's notes. `existing` rows use the editor's existing sentences (c4-editor-state.js). The words change only through the alignment review (CP-4), here and in c4-editor-uml-refusals.js together.

rows.sentence: Locked: ‹subject› or a part of it is given by the task, so it cannot be changed here.
rows.note: ‹subject› is an element's name as today, or "step 3 of ‹scenario›", "the steps of ‹scenario›", "node ‹name›", "the link from ‹A› to ‹B›", "the positions in this view", "the lifeline order in this view".

rows.sentence: The drawing changed before this edit was applied, so nothing was changed. Try again.
‹Name› is a ‹type› outside ‹Scope›. It is shown here because ‹Scope› works with it. Rename or delete it in ‹view title›.
This line ends at ‹Deep name›, a ‹type› inside ‹Box›, which this view draws as one box. Move or turn that end in ‹view title›, where ‹Deep name› is drawn.
‹A› and ‹B› are both outside ‹Scope›, so a line between them would not appear in this view. Add it in ‹view title›.

rows.summary: No notes in this design model
rows.sentence: This design model has no place for notes on a diagram. Write the explanation in the element's description.
Duplicating is not available here: every element has one identity in the model. Add a new element and name it.

rows.summary: Not recorded in this design model
rows.sentence: This design model records three kinds of line between code elements: extends, implements, and a collaborator, drawn as a dependency. It has no place for a composition, an aggregation, or an association, although UML has them. Draw a dependency and say what ‹Source› asks ‹Target› for.
‹Source› can extend or implement a code element. ‹Target› is a ‹type›.
rows.note: For a component it continues "Its classes and interfaces are in its code view."; for a container, system, or person, "Classes belong to the components inside a container."

rows.sentence: ‹Source› is ‹its kind› and ‹Target› is ‹its kind›. A class extends a class, and an interface extends an interface.
rows.note: Each kind with its article: "a class", "an interface". For a class and an interface it continues "To promise an interface's operations, draw a realization." Task 29 ruling (progress.md U6): a realization refused with extends-kind says "cannot implement".

rows.summary: Only an interface can be implemented
rows.sentence: ‹Target› is ‹its kind›. A class implements an interface; to build on a class, draw a generalization.
‹Target› already extends ‹Source›, so ‹Source› cannot extend ‹Target›.
The keyword shows the kind of this code element. Change its kind in the inspector.
A function is drawn with one operation, its own call. Edit the line to give it a signature; to remove it, change the element's kind.
A step runs along a relationship the design has, or answers an earlier request in this scenario. A step from ‹Sender› to ‹Receiver› does neither at this place.

‹Sender› has no relationship to ‹Receiver›, and no earlier step asks ‹Sender› for something it could answer. A scenario uses the collaborations the design has: ‹Sender› can answer an element that asked it earlier, or the message can go through an element that already works with ‹Receiver›.

‹Sender› can reply to ‹Receiver› only after an unanswered step from ‹Receiver› to ‹Sender›, earlier in this scenario or branch. A reply travels back along the request's relationship and needs none of its own.
rows.offer: Add the request from ‹Receiver› to ‹Sender› first…

rows.summary: No reply to an asynchronous message
rows.sentence: The relationship from ‹Receiver› to ‹Sender› is asynchronous: ‹Receiver› does not wait, so no reply travels back along it. If ‹Sender› must tell ‹Receiver› something, that is a collaboration of its own.
‹Child› is inside ‹Parent›. A step runs between two elements that are not inside each other.
A step runs between two elements. What ‹Name› does on its own belongs in its responsibilities.
A lifeline appears when a step uses its element. Choose Message, then the sender, then the receiver; Another element… lists the elements a step can reach from the sender.
Activation bars, create and destroy marks, and lost and found messages have no place in this design model's scenarios. A scenario records who asks whom for what, in order.

rows.summary: Not one of the five fragments
rows.sentence: A scenario in this design model has five fragments: alt, opt, loop, par, and break.
‹operator› has one branch. Use alt for alternatives or par for branches that run at the same time.
This is the fragment's only branch. Delete the fragment, or unwrap it to keep its steps.
A fragment cannot be moved into one of its own branches.

The arrow follows the model: solid for a call, dashed for a reply, an open arrowhead for a message, event, or stream. To change it, change the connector of the relationship this step runs along, or the step's direction.
This box shows that these lifelines belong to ‹Name›. It follows the model.

rows.summary: Host a container or system instead
rows.sentence: A deployment view of this design model shows which containers and software systems run on which nodes. It has no place for artifacts; host a container or a system on the node.
‹Node› is infrastructure, such as a load balancer: it hosts nothing and holds no nodes.
‹Node› cannot be moved into itself or into a node inside it.
‹Node› already hosts ‹Element›.
This path is drawn from the relationship from ‹Source› to ‹Target› (‹description›), because both run on these nodes. Change that relationship, or add a link between the two nodes.
A link joins two nodes. To show that two elements talk, add a relationship between them.

rows.summary: A node cannot link to itself
rows.sentence: A link joins two different nodes. What runs inside ‹Node› is shown by what it hosts and by the nodes inside it.
‹Node A› already has a link to ‹Node B›. Edit that link.
Both boxes are instances of ‹Element›, running on two nodes. To show that the instances talk to each other, add a link between ‹Node A› and ‹Node B›.
rows.offer: Add a link from ‹Node A› to ‹Node B›…

rows.sentence: ‹Name› is inside ‹Parent›, and what is inside a node is laid out for you. Move ‹Parent›, or use Move to… to put ‹Name› somewhere else.

rows.summary: Offer or use an interface instead
rows.sentence: This design model has no ports. An element offers an interface (a ball) and uses one (a socket).
This view shows ‹Scope› and the elements that share an interface with it. Add elements in a context, container, or component view; they appear here once they use or provide an interface.
‹Interface› is declared on ‹Owner›. Rename or remove it in the interfaces view of ‹Owner›.
‹Name› appears here because it ‹uses | provides› ‹Interface›. Delete that use, or delete the element in a context, container, or component view.

rows.summary: Delete it and draw the new one
rows.sentence: A line joins one use to one interface. To change it, delete this use and draw the new one.
The ball is on the side of the element that provides ‹Interface›. To turn the line around, describe an interface on ‹Consumer› and let ‹Provider› use it.
The label lists the operations ‹Consumer› uses. Change them under Uses in the relationship.
The line between a ball and its socket is routed for you, so the two stay joined. Move the elements to change it.
A ball or socket is placed for you, on the side of its element that faces the other end. Move the elements to turn it.
Generalization and realization lines are drawn as one tree for each parent, so they are routed for you. Move the elements to change them.
Two lines of this kind join ‹A› and ‹B›, so they are routed for you. Move the elements to change them.
Labels follow their lines here. Move a bend, or the elements the line joins.

extends-target.summary: Enrollment Policy is not a code element
extends-target.sentence: PrerequisiteRule can extend or implement a code element. Enrollment Policy is a component. Its classes and interfaces are in its code view.

extends-target.summary: Registration API is not a code element
extends-target.sentence: PrerequisiteRule can extend or implement a code element. Registration API is a container. Classes belong to the components inside a container.

extends-target.summary: Course Registration is not a code element
extends-target.sentence: PrerequisiteRule can extend or implement a code element. Course Registration is a software system. Classes belong to the components inside a container.

extends-target.summary: Student is not a code element
extends-target.sentence: PrerequisiteRule can extend or implement a code element. Student is a person. Classes belong to the components inside a container.

extends-kind.summary: A class cannot extend an interface
extends-kind.sentence: PrerequisiteRule is a class and EnrollmentRule is an interface. A class extends a class, and an interface extends an interface. To promise an interface's operations, draw a realization.

extends-kind.summary: An abstract class cannot extend an interface
extends-kind.sentence: RuleBase is an abstract class and EnrollmentRule is an interface. A class extends a class, and an interface extends an interface. To promise an interface's operations, draw a realization.

extends-kind.summary: An interface cannot extend a class
extends-kind.sentence: EnrollmentRule is an interface and EnrollmentPolicy is a class. A class extends a class, and an interface extends an interface.

extends-kind.summary: An enum cannot extend an abstract class
extends-kind.sentence: Grade is an enum and EnrollmentPolicy is an abstract class. A class extends a class, and an interface extends an interface.

extends-kind.summary: An interface cannot implement an interface
extends-kind.sentence: EnrollmentRule is an interface and Auditable is an interface. A class, an abstract class, or an enum implements an interface. To build on an interface, draw a generalization.

extends-kind.summary: A function cannot implement an interface
extends-kind.sentence: checkPrerequisites is a function and EnrollmentRule is an interface. A class, an abstract class, or an enum implements an interface.

implements-target.summary: Only an interface can be implemented
implements-target.sentence: EnrollmentPolicy is a class. A class implements an interface; to build on a class, draw a generalization.

implements-target.summary: Only an interface can be implemented
implements-target.sentence: Grade is an enum. A class implements an interface; to build on a class, draw a generalization.

interfaces/declared-elsewhere.sentence: Enrollment API is declared on Billing Gateway. Rename or remove it in the interfaces view of Billing Gateway.
Each element declares its own interfaces. Add one to Billing Gateway in the interfaces view of Billing Gateway.
